verses.zh: （大卫在献殿的时候，作这诗歌。）耶和华啊，我要尊崇你，因为你曾提拔我，不叫仇敌向我夸耀。
verses.en: A psalm, a song used at the dedication of the temple;[NOTE:1] by David.I will praise you, O Lord, for you lifted me up[NOTE:2] and did not allow my enemies to gloat[NOTE:3] over me.
notes: Psalm 30. The author thanks the Lord for delivering him from death and urges others to join him in praise. The psalmist experienced divine discipline for a brief time, but when he cried out for help the Lord intervened and restored his favor.

Heb “a song of the dedication of the house.” The referent of “house” is unclear. It is possible that David wrote this psalm for the dedication ceremony of Solomon’s temple. Another possibility is that the psalm was used on the occasion of the dedication of the second temple following the return from exile, or on the occasion of the rededication of the temple in Maccabean times.

Elsewhere the verb דָּלָה (dalah) is used of drawing water from a well (Exod 2:16, 19; Prov 20:5). The psalmist was trapped in the pit leading to Sheol (see v. 3), but the Lord hoisted him up. The Piel stem is used here, perhaps suggesting special exertion on the Lord’s part.

verses.zh: 耶和华―我的　神啊，我曾呼求你，你医治了我。
verses.en: O Lord my God,I cried out to you and you healed me.[NOTE:1]
notes: Or “rejoice.”

verses.zh: 耶和华啊，你曾把我的灵魂从阴间救上来，使我存活，不至于下坑。
verses.en: O Lord, you pulled me[NOTE:1] up from Sheol;you rescued me from among those descending into the grave.[NOTE:2]
notes: You healed me. Apparently the psalmist was plagued by a serious illness that threatened his life. See Ps 41.
Or “my life.”

verses.zh: 耶和华的圣民哪，你们要歌颂他，称赞他可记念的圣名。
verses.en: Sing to the Lord, you faithful followers[NOTE:1] of his;give thanks to his holy name.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “you kept me alive from those descending into the pit.” The Hebrew noun בּוֹר (bor, “pit, cistern”) is sometimes used of the grave and/or the realm of the dead. The translation follows the consonantal Hebrew text (Kethib); the marginal reading (Qere) has, “you kept me alive so that I did not go down into the pit.”
A “faithful follower” (חָסִיד) is one who does what is right in God’s eyes and remains faithful to God (see Pss 4:3; 12:1; 16:10; 31:23; 37:28; 86:2; 97:10).

verses.zh: 因为，他的怒气不过是转眼之间；他的恩典乃是一生之久。一宿虽然有哭泣，早晨便必欢呼。
verses.en: For his anger lasts only a brief moment,and his good favor restores one’s life.[NOTE:1] One may experience sorrow during the night,but joy arrives in the morning.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “to his holy remembrance.” The noun זֵכֵר (zekher, “remembrance”) here refers to the name of the Lord as invoked in liturgy and praise. Cf. Pss 6:5; 97:12. The Lord’s “name” is “holy” in the sense that it is a reminder of his uniqueness and greatness.

Heb “for [there is] a moment in his anger, [but] life in his favor.” Because of the parallelism with “moment,” some understand חַיִּים (khayyim) in a quantitative sense: “lifetime” (cf. NIV, NRSV). However, the immediate context, which emphasizes deliverance from death (see v. 3), suggests that חַיִּים has a qualitative sense: “physical life” or even “prosperous life” (cf. NEB “in his favour there is life”).

verses.zh: 至于我，我凡事平顺便说：我永不动摇。
verses.en: In my self-confidence I said,“I will never be shaken.”[NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “in the evening weeping comes to lodge, but at morning a shout of joy.” “Weeping” is personified here as a traveler who lodges with one temporarily.

verses.zh: 耶和华啊，你曾施恩，叫我的江山稳固；你掩了面，我就惊惶。
verses.en: O Lord, in your good favor you made me secure.[NOTE:1] Then you rejected me[NOTE:2] and I was terrified.
notes: In my self-confidence I said… Here the psalmist begins to fill in the background of the crisis referred to in the earlier verses. He had been arrogant and self-confident, so the Lord withdrew his protection and allowed trouble to invade his life (vv. 8-11).

Heb “in your good favor you caused to stand for my mountain strength.” Apparently this means “you established strength for my mountain” (“mountain” in this case representing his rule, which would be centered on Mt. Zion) or “you established strength as my mountain” (“mountain” in this case being a metaphor for security).

verses.zh: 耶和华啊，我曾求告你；我向耶和华恳求，说：
verses.en: To you, O Lord, I cried out;I begged the Lord for mercy:[NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “you hid your face.” The idiom “hide the face” can mean “ignore” (see Pss 10:11; 13:1; 51:9) or, as here, carry the stronger idea of “reject” (see Ps 88:14).

verses.zh: 我被害流血，下到坑中，有甚么益处呢？尘土岂能称赞你，传说你的诚实么？
verses.en: “What[NOTE:1] profit is there in taking my life,[NOTE:2] in my descending into the Pit?[NOTE:3] Can the dust of the grave[NOTE:4] praise you?Can it declare your loyalty?[NOTE:5]
notes: The prefixed verbal forms in v. 8 are probably preterites; the psalmist recalls that he prayed in his time of crisis.
The following two verses (vv. 9-10) contain the prayer (or an excerpt of the prayer) that the psalmist offered to the Lord during his crisis.
Heb “What profit [is there] in my blood?” “Blood” here represents his life.
The Hebrew term שָׁחַת (shakhat, “pit”) is often used as a title for Sheol (see Pss 16:10; 49:9; 55:24 HT [55:23 ET]; 103:4).
Heb “dust.” The words “of the grave” are supplied in the translation for clarification.

verses.zh: 耶和华啊，求你应允我，怜恤我！耶和华啊，求你帮助我！
verses.en: Hear, O Lord, and have mercy on me.O Lord, deliver me.”[NOTE:1]
notes: The rhetorical questions anticipate the answer, “Of course not!”sn According to the OT, those who descend into the realm of death/Sheol are cut off from God’s mighty deeds and from the worshiping covenant community that experiences divine intervention (Pss 6:5; 88:10-12; Isa 38:18). In his effort to elicit a positive divine response, the psalmist reminds God that he will receive no praise or glory if he allows the psalmist to die. Dead men do not praise God!

verses.zh: 你已将我的哀哭变为跳舞，将我的麻衣脱去，给我披上喜乐，
verses.en: Then you turned my lament into dancing;you removed my sackcloth and covered me with joy.[NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “be a helper to me.”

verses.zh: 好叫我的灵（原文是荣耀）歌颂你，并不住声。耶和华―我的　神啊，我要称谢你，直到永远！
verses.en: So now[NOTE:1] my heart[NOTE:2] will sing to you and not be silent;O Lord my God, I will always[NOTE:3] give thanks to you.
notes: Covered me with joy. “Joy” probably stands metonymically for festive attire here.
Heb “so that”; or “in order that.”

Heb “glory.” Some view כָבוֹד (khavod, “glory”) here as a metonymy for man’s inner being (see BDB 459 s.v. II כָּבוֹד 5), but it is preferable to emend the form to כְּבֵדִי (kevedi, “my liver”). Like the heart, the liver is viewed as the seat of one’s emotions. See also Pss 16:9; 57:9; 108:1, as well as H. W. Wolff, Anthropology of the Old Testament, 64, and M. Dahood, Psalms (AB), 1:90. For an Ugaritic example of the heart/liver as the source of joy, see G. R. Driver, Canaanite Myths and Legends, 47-48: “her [Anat’s] liver swelled with laughter, her heart was filled with joy, the liver of Anat with triumph.” “Heart” is used in the translation above for the sake of English idiom; the expression “my liver sings” would seem odd indeed to the modern reader.
